attribution: Original bounded CSS Vista skills teaching. Hypothetical examples are not evidence of real events. Grammar rules link to the existing course.

lessons.title: A complete sentence
lessons.explanation: A sentence expresses a complete thought. Find who or what the sentence is about, then what that subject does or is. An imperative may have an understood subject: you.
lessons.example: The researcher checked the figures. Subject: the researcher. Predicate: checked the figures.

check.prompt: Which sentence expresses a complete thought?
options: The committee published its report.
Because the report was late.
The report on the desk.
After checking the figures.
check.explanation: The subject committee has a finite verb, published, and the thought is complete.
option_feedback: The subject committee has a finite verb, published, and the thought is complete.
Because makes this clause dependent; it leaves the reader waiting for the main thought.
This noun phrase identifies a report but has no finite verb saying what it does or is.
After checking the figures is an introductory phrase, not a complete main clause.

lessons.task: Write one sentence about an action you completed today. Underline the subject mentally and identify its verb.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Subject and predicate
lessons.explanation: The subject identifies the person or thing discussed. The predicate says something about it. Extra words inside a subject do not change its head noun.
lessons.example: The books on the upper shelf belong to Sara. Books is the head noun; belong to Sara is the predicate.

check.prompt: Which is the head of the subject in "The quality of the reports matters"?
options: matters
quality of the reports
quality
reports
check.explanation: Quality is the head noun; of the reports describes it.
option_feedback: Matters is the predicate’s verb, not the head noun of the subject.
This is the whole subject phrase. The question asks for its head noun, quality.
Quality is the head noun; of the reports describes it.
Reports is inside the describing of phrase; quality controls agreement here.

lessons.task: Write a sentence whose subject includes an of phrase. Make the verb agree with the head noun.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Simple, compound and complex sentences
lessons.explanation: A simple sentence has one independent clause. A compound sentence joins independent clauses. A complex sentence includes an independent clause and at least one dependent clause. Length alone does not determine the type.
lessons.example: The class ended, but the students stayed. Both clauses can stand alone.

check.prompt: Which example is complex?
options: The students stayed.
The class ended, and the students stayed.
The class ended; the students stayed.
Although the class ended, the students stayed.
check.explanation: Although introduces a dependent clause; the students stayed is independent.
option_feedback: This contains one independent clause and no dependent clause, so it is simple.
And joins two independent clauses here, making a compound sentence.
The semicolon joins two independent clauses; neither is dependent, so this is compound.
Although introduces a dependent clause; the students stayed is independent.

lessons.task: Write a simple sentence, then revise it to show a condition using if or a contrast using although.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Repairing fragments
lessons.explanation: A dependent clause cannot normally stand alone in formal prose. Attach it to an independent clause, or remove the dependency while preserving meaning.
lessons.example: Fragment: Because the road was closed. Complete: We returned because the road was closed.

check.prompt: Which repair is complete?
options: The closed road near the village.
Although the road was closed.
We postponed the visit because the road was closed.
Because the road was closed.
check.explanation: The repair supplies an independent clause with a subject and a finite verb.
option_feedback: The noun phrase names a road but has no finite verb expressing a complete thought.
Although introduces a dependent clause and leaves the contrasting main thought unstated.
The repair supplies an independent clause with a subject and a finite verb.
Because still makes the clause dependent; it needs a main clause.

lessons.task: Repair this fragment in your own way: "Although the proposal was promising." Do not invent evidence about a real proposal.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Run-ons and comma splices
lessons.explanation: Two independent clauses need suitable punctuation or a conjunction. A comma alone usually cannot join them. Choose a boundary that reflects their relationship.
lessons.example: Comma splice: The room was crowded, we waited outside. Repair: The room was crowded, so we waited outside.

check.prompt: Which punctuation joins two related independent clauses correctly?
options: The draft is ready, the editor will review it.
The draft is ready the editor will review it.
The draft is ready; because the editor will review it.
The draft is ready; the editor will review it.
check.explanation: A semicolon can connect closely related independent clauses.
option_feedback: A comma alone splices these two independent clauses; use a suitable boundary or conjunction.
The independent clauses run together without punctuation or a connecting conjunction.
Because makes the second clause dependent, so it cannot stand after this semicolon as a second independent clause.
A semicolon can connect closely related independent clauses.

lessons.task: Repair "The instructions were unclear, we asked for help" using a connector that shows the relationship.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Subject–verb agreement
lessons.explanation: Match the verb to the head of the subject. A nearby plural noun inside a describing phrase does not make a singular subject plural.
lessons.example: The list of supplies is complete. List is singular.

check.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The purpose of these meetings are clear.
The purposes of this meeting is clear.
The purpose of these meetings were clear.
The purpose of these meetings is clear.
check.explanation: The singular head purpose requires is in this present-tense sentence.
option_feedback: Purpose is singular; the plural meetings inside the of phrase does not require are.
Purposes is plural, so the singular is does not agree with it.
Were does not agree with the singular purpose here; the stated present meaning also calls for is.
The singular head purpose requires is in this present-tense sentence.

lessons.task: Write a sentence beginning "The value of these lessons" and complete it with an appropriate verb.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Tense consistency
lessons.explanation: Keep the time frame clear. Tenses may change when the time changes, but an unexplained switch confuses the sequence.
lessons.example: Yesterday I revised the outline and checked the references. Both actions belong to yesterday.

check.prompt: Which sentence keeps its stated past time frame?
options: Last night, she draft the paragraph and review it.
Last night, she drafted the paragraph and reviewed it.
Last night, she drafts the paragraph and reviewed it.
Last night, she drafted the paragraph and reviews it.
check.explanation: Drafted and reviewed both refer to the stated past period.
option_feedback: Draft and review are bare forms here; this past sequence requires drafted and reviewed.
Drafted and reviewed both refer to the stated past period.
Drafts switches to present while reviewed and last night establish the past frame being tested.
Reviews switches to present within the stated past sequence; reviewed preserves that frame.

lessons.task: Describe two actions you completed yesterday in one sentence. Keep both verbs consistent with that time.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Clear word order
lessons.explanation: Put words near what they describe. Keep the main subject and verb easy to locate. Position only carefully because it can limit different parts of a sentence.
lessons.example: Only Mina submitted a draft means nobody else did. Mina submitted only a draft means she submitted nothing else.

check.prompt: Which sentence places only immediately before the submitted item?
options: Mina only submitted a draft.
Mina submitted a draft only to the editor.
Mina submitted only a draft.
Only Mina submitted a draft.
check.explanation: Only directly before a draft limits the item submitted.
option_feedback: Only is immediately before submitted. Its scope may depend on emphasis, but it is not in the position the question asks for.
Only is immediately before to the editor, limiting the recipient rather than the submitted item.
Only directly before a draft limits the item submitted.
Only is immediately before Mina, limiting who submitted rather than the submitted item.

lessons.task: Write two sentences with only in different positions, then explain how their meanings differ.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Misplaced and dangling modifiers
lessons.explanation: An opening participial phrase should describe the subject that follows. Otherwise the sentence may appear to assign an action to an object.
lessons.example: Dangling: Walking to class, the rain soaked me. Clear: Walking to class, I was soaked by the rain.

check.prompt: Which sentence avoids a dangling modifier?
options: After reviewing the figures, the report seemed clearer.
After reviewing the figures, the researcher corrected the table.
After reviewing the figures, the table was corrected.
After reviewing the figures, several errors appeared.
check.explanation: The researcher is the person who reviewed the figures.
option_feedback: The report becomes the apparent reviewer; clearer wording must identify the person who reviewed the figures.
The researcher is the person who reviewed the figures.
The table becomes the apparent reviewer, although the table cannot review the figures. Name the reviewer as the subject.
Several errors becomes the apparent reviewer. The opening phrase needs the person who reviewed as its subject.

lessons.task: Repair "After reading the instructions, the task became easier" by naming the person who read.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Parallel structure
lessons.explanation: Use matching grammatical forms for ideas presented as equals. Parallel structure helps readers recognize the relationship without reinterpreting the syntax.
lessons.example: The workshop teaches planning, drafting and revising. Each item is an -ing form.

check.prompt: Which list is parallel?
options: We aim to improving access, reduce delays and explain decisions.
We aim to improve access, delays and explaining decisions.
We aim to improve access, reduce delays and explain decisions.
We aim to improve access, reducing delays and decisions explained.
check.explanation: The coordinated verbs improve, reduce and explain share the same to.
option_feedback: Aim to requires an infinitive here; improving does not match reduce and explain.
The list mixes improve access, the noun delays and explaining decisions instead of matching coordinated verb phrases.
The coordinated verbs improve, reduce and explain share the same to.
Improve, reducing and decisions explained do not share a grammatical form in this coordinated list.

lessons.task: Rewrite "The programme encourages reading, to discuss ideas and revision" with matching forms.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Cause, contrast and condition
lessons.explanation: Choose a connector that expresses the intended logic. Because gives a reason; although introduces contrast; if introduces a condition. These relationships are not interchangeable.
lessons.example: If the library extends its hours, more evening study may be possible. This is conditional, not a promise.

check.prompt: Which connector introduces a condition?
options: because
although
therefore
if
check.explanation: If sets a condition on the following claim.
option_feedback: Because introduces a reason, not the condition on which a claim depends.
Although signals a contrast or concession rather than a condition.
Therefore signals an inference or result; it does not introduce a conditional clause.
If sets a condition on the following claim.

lessons.task: Write three short sentences about a hypothetical study plan: one cause, one contrast and one condition.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Connectors and transitions
lessons.explanation: A transition must match the relationship between ideas. However signals contrast; therefore signals a conclusion; for example introduces an illustration. Punctuation still needs to be correct.
lessons.example: The first route is shorter. However, the second route has fewer obstacles.

check.prompt: Which transition best signals an illustration?
options: for example
nevertheless
therefore
in contrast
check.explanation: For example introduces an instance of the preceding general idea.
option_feedback: For example introduces an instance of the preceding general idea.
Nevertheless introduces a concession or contrast, not an illustration of a general point.
Therefore signals a conclusion or consequence rather than an example.
In contrast points to a difference between ideas, not an illustration.

lessons.task: Write a general statement about a study habit and add an illustrative sentence with an appropriate transition.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Concision and redundancy
lessons.explanation: Remove words that repeat a meaning without removing necessary conditions or distinctions. Concision is faithful compression, not merely making a sentence shorter.
lessons.example: At this point in time can usually become now. A future possibility can often become a possibility.

check.prompt: Which revision keeps the meaning of "The reason for the delay is that the file is missing"?
options: The file is missing, causing the delay.
The file is missing.
The missing file may have caused the delay.
The delay caused the file to go missing.
check.explanation: The revision retains both the missing file and its stated causal relationship to the delay.
option_feedback: The revision retains both the missing file and its stated causal relationship to the delay.
This retains the missing file but omits its stated role as the reason for the delay.
May have caused changes the original stated causal relationship into a tentative past possibility.
This reverses the causal direction: the original says the missing file caused the delay.

lessons.task: Shorten "It is necessary for students to make a plan in advance before they begin" without losing its instruction.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Clarity and precision
lessons.explanation: Identify what vague words refer to. Replace a vague noun or pronoun when the context permits, but do not manufacture details the writer has not supplied.
lessons.example: Vague: This improved things. Clear, with known context: The new timetable reduced missed classes.

check.prompt: What should an editor do when "this" has no clear referent?
options: Replace this with the matter while leaving the referent unspecified.
Remove this and the claim it introduces without checking the intended meaning.
Ask which idea or action the writer means.
Choose the most likely referent without asking the writer.
check.explanation: Clarification preserves the writer’s meaning instead of inventing it.
option_feedback: The matter remains unspecified; a different vague expression does not resolve the reference.
Deleting the claim may remove intended meaning. Clarify the reference before deciding how to revise it.
Clarification preserves the writer’s meaning instead of inventing it.
Guessing a likely referent risks replacing the writer’s intention with the editor’s assumption.

lessons.task: Write a vague sentence with this or things, then replace the vague expression using only details you actually intend.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Word choice and academic tone
lessons.explanation: Use accurate, proportionate wording. Formal writing does not require rare words or hostility. Avoid absolute labels when your evidence supports only a qualified criticism.
lessons.example: Overstated: The proposal is totally useless. Precise: The proposal does not address the stated implementation problem.

check.prompt: Which option offers a measured criticism?
options: The argument overlooks the cost of implementation.
The argument cannot possibly contribute anything useful.
The writer is incapable of understanding implementation.
Every argument for reform necessarily ignores implementation costs.
check.explanation: The criticism identifies a specific limitation without personal insult or an unsupported universal claim.
option_feedback: The criticism identifies a specific limitation without personal insult or an unsupported universal claim.
Cannot possibly contribute anything dismisses the whole argument instead of identifying a supported limitation.
This attacks the writer’s ability rather than explaining a specific weakness in the argument.
Every and necessarily make an unsupported universal claim rather than a measured criticism of this argument.

lessons.task: Rewrite "This idea is really bad" as a specific criticism of a hypothetical idea, clearly stating the limitation.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Expressing cause and effect
lessons.explanation: Separate an observed association from a causal explanation. State the proposed mechanism and relevant condition. Use can or may when the claim is conditional.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: If unclear instructions delay decisions, clarifying responsibilities may reduce that delay.

check.prompt: Which sentence makes a conditional causal claim?
options: Decisions slowed after responsibilities changed, which proves that the change caused the slowdown.
The offices have unclear responsibilities and record delayed decisions.
Unclear responsibilities may delay decisions when approvals are required from several offices.
Unclear responsibilities inevitably delay every decision.
check.explanation: The sentence proposes an outcome and a condition without claiming inevitability.
option_feedback: Sequence alone does not prove causation. The statement excludes other explanations without support.
This records two conditions together but does not explain a causal relationship or state a condition for it.
The sentence proposes an outcome and a condition without claiming inevitability.
Inevitably and every assert an unconditional result; the question asks for a conditional causal claim.

lessons.task: Construct a causal sentence about a hypothetical administrative delay. Include a mechanism and a qualification.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Building an argumentative sentence
lessons.explanation: Make a defensible claim, give a relevant reason and indicate the condition under which it applies. A strong sentence does more than announce a preference.
lessons.example: A trial of extended study hours is worth considering if evening access is a barrier, because it would test whether access improves attendance.

check.prompt: Which sentence gives a claim supported by relevant reasoning?
options: The timetable should be reviewed because it should be reviewed.
The timetable should be reviewed because its printed layout looks dated.
The timetable should be reviewed because two compulsory classes currently overlap.
The timetable should be reviewed because printing the same timetable on cheaper paper would save money.
check.explanation: Overlapping compulsory classes is a relevant reason for reviewing a timetable.
option_feedback: The reason repeats the conclusion, so it provides no independent support for reviewing the timetable.
A dated printed layout does not explain a scheduling problem; it supports redesigning the presentation rather than the timetable itself.
Overlapping compulsory classes is a relevant reason for reviewing a timetable.
Cheaper paper supports a change to printing costs, not a change to the timetable’s schedule.

lessons.task: Write a claim about a hypothetical classroom improvement and support it with one relevant reason.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Building an analytical sentence
lessons.explanation: Show how or why an outcome could arise. Name a mechanism, condition or competing explanation. Description tells what; analysis examines the relationship.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: A longer journey could reduce attendance by making punctual arrival harder, although class timing might also explain absences.

check.prompt: Which statement offers analysis rather than only description?
options: The library opens at the same time each weekday.
The opening timetable lists five weekday sessions.
The library opening time is inconvenient.
A fixed opening time may restrict access for students whose classes finish later.
check.explanation: It links opening time to a possible mechanism affecting a defined group.
option_feedback: This describes a schedule without explaining how it affects access or another outcome.
This counts listed sessions without explaining a mechanism or relationship.
This expresses a judgement but does not explain who is affected or how the time creates a problem.
It links opening time to a possible mechanism affecting a defined group.

lessons.task: Write one analytical sentence about a hypothetical access problem, including an alternative explanation.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Qualification without vagueness
lessons.explanation: A qualification states the scope or condition of a claim. It should make the statement more precise rather than weaken every verb with several uncertain expressions.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: The shorter route is preferable when travel time matters more than shelter.

check.prompt: Which statement has a clear condition?
options: The shorter route is preferable when both routes are equally safe.
The shorter route might perhaps be preferable in some unspecified situations.
The shorter route is preferable regardless of the routes’ safety.
The shorter route is preferable because I like it.
check.explanation: The condition specifies the circumstances in which the comparison holds.
option_feedback: The condition specifies the circumstances in which the comparison holds.
The repeated hedges leave the relevant situations unspecified instead of naming a clear condition.
Regardless of safety removes a relevant condition instead of defining when the preference applies.
Personal preference gives a reason for liking the route but no explicit condition delimiting the claim.

lessons.task: Make "Online discussion improves participation" into a qualified hypothesis without inventing supporting data.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Advanced sentence transformation
lessons.explanation: Change structure while preserving who acts, what is claimed, the time frame and qualifications. A passive construction or compressed clause must not strengthen the original claim.
lessons.example: Original: The team may finish the review if the missing files arrive. Equivalent: The review may be finished by the team if the missing files arrive.

check.prompt: Which revision preserves "The measure may reduce delays if staff receive training"?
options: Staff training has already enabled the measure to reduce delays.
The measure may reduce delays whether or not staff receive training.
With staff training, the measure may reduce delays.
With staff training, the measure will reduce delays.
check.explanation: May and the training condition remain; neither certainty nor timing is invented.
option_feedback: Has already changes a conditional possibility into an asserted completed result.
Whether or not training occurs removes the original training condition and changes the claim.
May and the training condition remain; neither certainty nor timing is invented.
Will replaces may with certainty; the conditional possibility in the original must remain.

lessons.task: Transform a conditional sentence of your own into a different structure. Check that its qualification and meaning survive.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and word choice
lessons.explanation: Choose words for their meaning and natural use in context. Similar dictionary meanings do not make words interchangeable. Check what a replacement would add, remove or imply.
lessons.example: Effective concerns achieving an intended result; efficient concerns the resources used. A measure may be effective but costly. Decide which judgement you intend before choosing either word.

check.prompt: Which sentence preserves the meaning "These figures do not provide enough support for the claim"?
options: These figures make the claim unlikely.
These figures are insufficient to support the claim.
These figures disprove the claim.
These figures confirm the claim.
check.explanation: Insufficient means not enough. Lack of enough support does not establish that the opposite claim is true.
option_feedback: Not enough support does not by itself establish that the claim is unlikely; that judgement needs further grounds.
Insufficient means not enough. Lack of enough support does not establish that the opposite claim is true.
Insufficient support does not show that the claim is false; disprove strengthens the original meaning.
Confirm reverses the original judgement that the figures do not provide enough support.

lessons.task: Write a sentence using effective or efficient. Explain the meaning you intend and test an alternative word against it.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Fact, opinion and argument
lessons.explanation: A factual claim can be checked; an opinion expresses a judgement; an argument offers reasons for a conclusion. A factual-looking claim may still be unverified.
lessons.example: Hypothetical opinion: I prefer longer library hours. Argument: The library should trial longer hours because some classes end after it closes.

check.prompt: Which is an argument?
options: The timetable should change because two required classes overlap.
The timetable is convenient.
Two required classes overlap.
The timetable should change.
check.explanation: The timetable proposal gives a conclusion and a relevant reason.
option_feedback: The timetable proposal gives a conclusion and a relevant reason.
This is an evaluation without a supporting reason.
This is a checkable premise, but it does not itself state a proposal and supporting reason.
This states a conclusion without explaining why it should be accepted.

lessons.task: In a hypothetical school, distinguish a checkable statement, a personal preference and a reasoned proposal about its timetable. Write one of each. Label any factual-looking statement that you have not verified.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Finding a central claim
lessons.explanation: A central claim states what you want a reader to accept. Keep it specific enough to challenge and distinguish it from the topic.
lessons.example: Topic: classroom access. Claim: A trial evening session could improve access for students with late classes.

check.prompt: Which is a claim rather than only a topic?
options: The advantages of a study session.
The school should trial an evening study session.
Possible evening study arrangements.
Access for students whose classes end late.
check.explanation: The sentence proposes a position that can be supported or challenged.
option_feedback: This announces a discussion rather than a defensible position.
The sentence proposes a position that can be supported or challenged.
This names a topic rather than taking a position.
This identifies an issue or group, but does not state what should be accepted.

lessons.task: A hypothetical school has one unused room. State a specific proposal for using it, then distinguish your central claim from the general topic and from a reason supporting it.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Relevant supporting reasons
lessons.explanation: A reason supports a claim only when it helps explain why the conclusion should be accepted. A true but unrelated statement is not useful support.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: Repairing a broken light is relevant to safe evening use; the colour of the noticeboard is not.

check.prompt: Which reason directly connects repairing the light to seeing classroom material?
options: Repairing the light would be easier than changing the timetable.
The classroom is used by several subjects.
The room has recently been repainted.
Students cannot read the board clearly in that room.
check.explanation: Visibility bears directly on the purpose of the repair.
option_feedback: Ease of implementation does not explain the visibility benefit being asked about.
Frequent use alone does not establish how the broken light affects seeing the material.
A room improvement does not explain why its lighting needs repair.
Visibility bears directly on the purpose of the repair.

lessons.task: A hypothetical classroom light is broken. Give one reason that connects repairing it to learning in that room. Contrast it with a genuine concern that does not establish that particular benefit.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Explaining the link
lessons.explanation: Explain the link between the reason and the claim. Naming two ideas beside each other does not show why one supports the other.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: Moving a class avoids the overlap, so students can attend both required sessions.

check.prompt: Which sentence explains the reason–claim link?
options: The overlap is inconvenient, and the new timetable would look clearer.
Students favour the change, so it will remove every attendance difficulty.
Moving one class would remove the overlap and allow attendance at both.
Moving the class is the appropriate change because it should be moved.
check.explanation: It names the mechanism by which the proposed change helps.
option_feedback: Naming a problem and a different benefit does not explain the attendance mechanism.
Preference does not establish either the mechanism or that all barriers disappear.
It names the mechanism by which the proposed change helps.
This restates the proposal rather than explaining how it helps.

lessons.task: Suppose two required sessions overlap. Propose a scheduling change, then explain step by step how it would remove that specific barrier. State one condition under which your solution would still fail.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Selecting evidence
lessons.explanation: Choose evidence that bears on the claim and has an identifiable source, date and scope. An illustrative example is not proof of a general claim.
lessons.example: To examine library access, collect opening times and actual student schedules; a fictional example only explains the question.

check.prompt: Which evidence is most directly relevant to a claimed timetable overlap?
options: The dated timetables for both required classes.
A dated timetable for only one of the two classes.
A teacher availability list without the scheduled class times.
Student opinions about whether the timetable is convenient.
check.explanation: The actual timetables can establish whether those class times overlap.
option_feedback: The actual timetables can establish whether those class times overlap.
A comparison requires the relevant times of both classes.
Availability does not establish when those classes actually occur.
Opinions can identify a concern, but they do not directly establish the claimed overlap.

lessons.task: Investigate a hypothetical claim that two required classes overlap. Name the actual records needed, their dates and what you would compare. Explain why preferences alone cannot establish their timing.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Premises and conclusions
lessons.explanation: Premises are the supporting statements; the conclusion is what they are meant to establish. Check whether accepting the premises really supports that conclusion.
lessons.example: All required classes must be attendable. Two required classes overlap. Therefore, the timetable needs review. This identifies a conflict, without proving a particular remedy.

check.prompt: What is the conclusion in that example?
options: Every class must move to the evening.
The timetable needs review.
Two required classes overlap.
All required classes must be attendable.
check.explanation: Needs review is the judgement supported by the premises.
option_feedback: This particular remedy does not follow from the stated premises.
Needs review is the judgement supported by the premises.
This is a supporting premise, not the resulting judgement.
This is the standard used as a premise.

lessons.task: A hypothetical centre says all required workshops must be attendable, but two workshops overlap. Write the premises and the conclusion they support. Explain why these premises do not select one particular remedy.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Identifying assumptions
lessons.explanation: An assumption is a step your reasoning relies on without establishing it. Name it and ask what happens if it is false.
lessons.example: A longer opening period will help only if affected students can and wish to use it.

check.prompt: Which assumption directly connects evening hours to the affected students gaining access?
options: A longer opening period necessarily lowers the staffing cost.
Current morning users prefer the existing timetable.
A published notice is sufficient to remove every access barrier.
Affected students can use the proposed evening hours.
check.explanation: Potential access depends on whether the relevant students can actually attend.
option_feedback: A cost claim is not the access assumption, and a longer period does not establish lower cost.
Their preference does not establish whether the affected evening users can attend.
Information alone does not establish practical ability to use the proposed hours.
Potential access depends on whether the relevant students can actually attend.

lessons.task: A hypothetical library proposes evening access. Identify an assumption linking the new hours to the intended users. Explain what observation would challenge it and how that would qualify your proposal.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Cause-and-effect arguments
lessons.explanation: A causal argument needs a mechanism, timing and consideration of alternative causes. Events occurring together do not by themselves establish causation.
lessons.example: Hypothetical: If unclear approval responsibility delays a task, naming a responsible officer may reduce that delay.

check.prompt: Why is "attendance rose after the notice, so the notice caused the rise" incomplete?
options: Other changes could explain the rise.
The order of events already identifies the notice as the cause.
A plausible explanation is sufficient without checking competing changes.
The attendance increase itself shows which change produced it.
check.explanation: The sequence is compatible with causation but does not exclude other explanations.
option_feedback: The sequence is compatible with causation but does not exclude other explanations.
Earlier occurrence is compatible with causation but does not exclude other causes.
A mechanism needs assessment, not just plausibility.
An outcome alone cannot identify one cause among several possible changes.

lessons.task: Suppose attendance improves after a hypothetical schedule change. Explain a possible mechanism, identify a competing explanation and describe evidence that could distinguish them. Treat the improvement as part of the scenario, not a real finding.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Recognising common fallacies
lessons.explanation: A personal attack does not refute reasoning. A false dilemma excludes alternatives without justification. Circular reasoning restates the claim as its reason.
lessons.example: Circular: This plan is best because no plan is better. That supplies no independent support.

check.prompt: Which statement is circular?
options: The rule is justified because it is a justified rule.
The rule is justified because the administrator favours it.
The rule needs review because it conflicts with another requirement.
The rule is justified because its wording is polished.
check.explanation: The reason merely repeats the conclusion.
option_feedback: The reason merely repeats the conclusion.
This appeals to a person rather than simply restating the conclusion; it is not the circular example.
This supplies a distinct reason that can be examined.
This substitutes presentation for support, rather than repeating the conclusion.

lessons.task: For a hypothetical school policy, write examples of a personal attack, a false dilemma and circular reasoning. Explain the fault in each, then replace one faulty reason with independent relevant support.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Weak and irrelevant arguments
lessons.explanation: Separate a reason that fails from a conclusion that may still be true. Rejecting one bad argument does not automatically prove the opposite conclusion.
lessons.example: An irrelevant colour preference does not support extending library hours, but it does not prove that hours should remain unchanged.

check.prompt: What follows when a reason is irrelevant?
options: The opposite claim is established by the failure of this reason.
No other reason could support the claim.
More confident wording would make the reason support the claim.
That reason does not support the claim.
check.explanation: Failure of support is not proof of the opposite position.
option_feedback: Failure of one support does not establish the opposite claim.
One irrelevant reason does not exclude different relevant evidence.
Confidence does not repair the lack of logical relevance.
Failure of support is not proof of the opposite position.

lessons.task: Someone supports extending a hypothetical library timetable with an irrelevant reason. Explain why that reason fails without declaring the proposal false. Give a separate relevant reason that still needs verification.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Constructing a counterargument
lessons.explanation: Present a serious opposing reason in a form an informed opponent might accept. Do not make the opposing view weaker for convenience.
lessons.example: A concern about longer library hours could be staffing cost and the reliability of supervision.

check.prompt: Which counterargument engages an access proposal seriously?
options: Longer hours may require staffing resources that are unavailable.
Longer hours could give late-class students more access.
The proposal is attractive because learning matters.
The school can decide how to advertise the new hours.
check.explanation: It identifies a practical constraint relevant to the proposal.
option_feedback: It identifies a practical constraint relevant to the proposal.
This supports the proposal rather than raising a counterargument.
A favourable general statement does not engage an opposing constraint.
Advertising does not address whether the required staffing exists.

lessons.task: Defend a hypothetical evening study session, then formulate the strongest reasonable objection about staffing or equitable access. Explain the objection in terms its proponent could accept before attempting a reply.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Responding with a rebuttal
lessons.explanation: Answer the actual opposing reason. Concede what is valid, show what evidence is needed and explain why your position remains defensible under stated conditions.
lessons.example: A limited trial could test demand within an agreed staffing budget; it cannot guarantee that costs disappear.

check.prompt: Which reply addresses a staffing-cost objection?
options: Treat expressed demand as proof that staffing can be funded.
Promise that efficiency will cover the cost without checking the budget.
Trial limited hours within a stated budget, then compare demand and cost.
Present the educational benefits again without discussing staffing.
check.explanation: The reply directly addresses the constraint and proposes a test rather than inventing savings.
option_feedback: Demand and available funding are different matters.
An unverified saving does not answer the resource constraint.
The reply directly addresses the constraint and proposes a test rather than inventing savings.
Repeating benefits leaves the cost objection unanswered.

lessons.task: A hypothetical digital study tool is challenged on privacy grounds. State the objection fairly, concede a valid concern and propose a bounded response. Explain what handling or retention evidence must be checked before adoption.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Qualification and nuance
lessons.explanation: State where your claim applies and where it may fail. A qualified claim can be stronger because its scope matches its reasons and evidence.
lessons.example: A trial is defensible if supervision and staffing are available; otherwise another access arrangement may be preferable.

check.prompt: Which claim is appropriately qualified?
options: A trial is worthwhile whenever any demand exists, regardless of resources.
No conclusion can be reached until every uncertainty is eliminated.
A successful trial in one setting establishes success in every setting.
A trial may be useful where staffing and demand justify it.
check.explanation: The qualification connects the claim to relevant conditions.
option_feedback: Demand alone does not satisfy the stated staffing condition.
Qualification permits a bounded judgement despite remaining uncertainty.
A limited observation cannot establish universal applicability.
The qualification connects the claim to relevant conditions.

lessons.task: Develop a qualified claim about a hypothetical distance-learning option. State who might benefit, the access conditions required and a case in which your claim would not apply. Do not invent results.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Developing an argumentative paragraph
lessons.explanation: Organise a paragraph around one claim, explain the reason, identify suitable evidence and relate it back to the claim. Avoid a list of disconnected slogans.
lessons.example: Plan: claim about access → mechanism → evidence needed → limitation → qualified conclusion. This is a structure, not a supplied argument.

check.prompt: Which item should explain why evidence supports the claim?
options: A repetition of the evidence in stronger wording.
A source label without explaining its relevance.
The reasoning linking the evidence to the claim.
A second claim stated immediately after the evidence.
check.explanation: Readers need the inferential connection, not merely a pasted fact.
option_feedback: Repetition does not provide the inferential connection.
Attribution matters, but a label alone does not explain the evidence–claim link.
Readers need the inferential connection, not merely a pasted fact.
Another claim does not explain how the evidence supports the first one.

lessons.task: Write one hypothetical policy paragraph with a controlling claim, a supporting reason, an explicit evidence need and a qualification. Explain the inferential role of each part instead of adding an unsupported quotation.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Evaluating a complete argument
lessons.explanation: Review relevance, clarity, logical consistency, reasoning, evidence, alternatives, rebuttal and coherence. These instructional criteria are not examiner marks.
lessons.example: A defensible argument may still need better evidence; do not confuse fluent language with a sound inference.

check.prompt: Which review is most useful?
options: Treat a supplied reference as verified without examining its source.
Correct the vocabulary and assume the reasoning is therefore sound.
Count supporting statements without checking whether they are relevant.
Identify a specific inference or evidence gap and explain how to test it.
check.explanation: Specific criticism helps the writer revise a real weakness.
option_feedback: A reference must be checked before it is accepted as reliable support.
Language improvement alone does not validate the inference.
The number of statements does not establish the quality of their support.
Specific criticism helps the writer revise a real weakness.

lessons.task: Evaluate your own hypothetical argument: identify its weakest inference, an unsupported premise and a serious alternative. Revise the argument to address one weakness while retaining any unresolved limitation. Use qualitative criticism, not examination marks.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Description and analysis
lessons.explanation: Description states what happens. Analysis examines how, why or under what conditions it happens. Neither permits inventing evidence.
lessons.example: Description: A school uses an online form. Analysis question: How could the form change the time needed to process a request?

check.prompt: Which question is analytical?
options: When was the form introduced?
How might the form alter processing time?
Which fields does the form contain?
How many requests were entered?
check.explanation: It asks about a mechanism connecting a change to an outcome.
option_feedback: A date describes timing without examining the proposed mechanism.
It asks about a mechanism connecting a change to an outcome.
This asks for a description of its contents.
A count describes activity; it does not by itself explain how the form changes processing time.

lessons.task: A hypothetical office replaces a paper request form with an online form. First describe the change. Then ask and answer a mechanism question about processing time, clearly distinguishing a hypothesis from established evidence.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Causes and consequences
lessons.explanation: Separate a proposed cause from its consequences. Explain the intermediate steps, then identify what would need checking.
lessons.example: Hypothetical chain: unclear instructions → repeated queries → delayed completion. Each link needs evidence.

check.prompt: What should be added to a list of causes?
options: A description of the outcome repeated after each cause.
An explanation of how each could produce the outcome.
A longer list of causes without explaining the links.
A decision that whichever cause is listed first must be strongest.
check.explanation: Analysis explains links rather than merely naming possible causes.
option_feedback: Repeating the outcome does not explain the intermediate steps.
Analysis explains links rather than merely naming possible causes.
Adding names does not show how a cause produces the outcome.
List order does not establish causal importance.

lessons.task: Analyse a hypothetical sequence of unclear instructions, repeated queries and delayed completion. Explain each proposed link, identify a point where the sequence could fail and name observations needed to test it.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Relationships between variables
lessons.explanation: A variable is a quantity or characteristic that can differ. Ask how a change in one might relate to another, and whether conditions alter that relationship.
lessons.example: Hypothetical variables: travel time and attendance. A relationship could differ with transport reliability.

check.prompt: Which pair contains the proposed explanatory variable and outcome in the travel-and-attendance example?
options: Travel time and transport reliability.
Attendance and the date a register was copied.
Transport reliability and journey duration.
Travel time and attendance.
check.explanation: The pair allows a relationship to be examined rather than assumed.
option_feedback: Reliability is a possible condition; this pair omits the attendance outcome.
This pair includes the outcome but not the proposed travel-time explanatory variable.
This pair examines transport conditions but omits the stated attendance outcome.
The pair allows a relationship to be examined rather than assumed.

lessons.task: Consider travel time and class attendance in a hypothetical school. Identify the proposed explanatory variable, the outcome and a condition such as transport reliability. Explain why the proposed relationship still needs evidence.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Recognising assumptions
lessons.explanation: Identify a step taken for granted. Ask whether it is necessary and what evidence could support or challenge it.
lessons.example: An online service helps only if users have the access and skills needed to use it.

check.prompt: What assumption underlies a claim that online forms improve everyone’s access?
options: Everyone concerned can access and use the form.
The office prefers receiving online requests.
The form has fewer fields than the previous version.
People who already use online services prefer the form.
check.explanation: The universal claim relies on access and usability, which need checking.
option_feedback: The universal claim relies on access and usability, which need checking.
An institutional preference does not establish access for every user.
A shorter form does not establish that all users can access and use it.
The views of existing users do not establish the circumstances of everyone concerned.

lessons.task: A hypothetical office claims its online form improves access for everyone. Identify what this assumes about access and skills. Describe a counterexample and explain how it would narrow the claim.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Evaluating evidence
lessons.explanation: Consider source, date, method, population and relevance. A small self-selected response does not automatically represent everyone.
lessons.example: A voluntary class survey may reveal respondents’ views but cannot alone establish the whole school’s preferences.

check.prompt: What limitation should be noted for a voluntary survey?
options: A large response count automatically makes the sample representative.
Written answers establish that preferences will remain unchanged.
Using one question guarantees that everyone is equally likely to respond.
Respondents may differ from nonrespondents.
check.explanation: Selection can affect what the findings represent.
option_feedback: Sample size does not by itself resolve self-selection.
Recording current views does not establish their future stability.
A common question does not guarantee equal participation.
Selection can affect what the findings represent.

lessons.task: Review a hypothetical voluntary survey about a study service. Identify its population, how participants joined and whose views could be missing. State what it can suggest and what it cannot establish about all students.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Competing explanations
lessons.explanation: Develop plausible alternatives and ask what observations could distinguish them. Do not list alternatives and then ignore them.
lessons.example: Absence could relate to travel, class timing or illness; different records would help distinguish these explanations.

check.prompt: What makes an alternative explanation useful?
options: A clear prediction that can be compared with observations.
Compatibility with one observation, without distinguishing the rival explanation.
Agreement with the explanation the writer already prefers.
A broader label that cannot be checked against any observation.
check.explanation: A discriminating prediction helps test competing explanations.
option_feedback: A discriminating prediction helps test competing explanations.
Both explanations may fit that observation; a useful test distinguishes them.
Preference does not make an alternative informative.
An untestable label cannot help distinguish the proposed causes.

lessons.task: Suppose a hypothetical office has long queues. Compare a staffing explanation with an approval-rule explanation. Identify an observation that would favour one over the other, rather than merely listing both.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Correlation and causation
lessons.explanation: Association does not establish causal direction or exclude a third factor. Examine mechanism, sequence and competing explanations.
lessons.example: Two outcomes might both change after a timetable revision; this does not alone show that one caused the other.

check.prompt: What could explain an observed association besides direct causation?
options: The first measured variable must cause the second one.
The association rules out a factor affecting both variables.
A third factor affecting both variables.
The stronger association must identify the direction of causation.
check.explanation: A common cause can produce association without direct causation between the measured variables.
option_feedback: The order of measurement does not establish the order of causes.
Association does not rule out a common cause.
A common cause can produce association without direct causation between the measured variables.
Strength alone does not establish causal direction.

lessons.task: In a hypothetical school, attendance and punctuality both improve during one term. Examine direct causation, reverse causation and a possible common cause. Describe what timing or comparison evidence would be needed before attributing an effect.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Institutional and structural factors
lessons.explanation: Look beyond individual intention to rules, resources, responsibilities and incentives. These factors are possible explanations, not excuses or automatic causes.
lessons.example: A request may wait because no office has a clear approval responsibility, even when individuals want to help.

check.prompt: Which is an institutional factor?
options: One applicant feels frustrated by waiting.
An officer personally hopes to finish the task quickly.
The observer thinks the building looks inefficient.
The rule assigning approval responsibility.
check.explanation: The rule governs how the institution processes decisions.
option_feedback: This describes a personal response rather than the institutional rule asked about.
An intention does not specify the allocation of institutional responsibility.
An impression of the building does not identify an operating institutional factor.
The rule governs how the institution processes decisions.

lessons.task: A hypothetical permit request passes between offices without a decision. Analyse responsibilities, rules and resources separately from individual intentions. Explain one proposed mechanism and the records needed to test it.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Analysing multiple dimensions
lessons.explanation: Choose dimensions relevant to the issue: resources, implementation, distribution, incentives or rights. More headings do not help unless each affects the reasoning.
lessons.example: A hypothetical education initiative can be examined for access, teaching capacity, cost and unequal effects.

check.prompt: When should a dimension be included?
options: When it produces the longest section in the response.
When it changes an explanation, consequence or judgement.
When it supplies another heading, even without affecting the argument.
When it repeats an existing dimension under a new label.
check.explanation: Relevant dimensions deepen reasoning; unrelated headings add clutter.
option_feedback: Length does not establish relevance to the issue.
Relevant dimensions deepen reasoning; unrelated headings add clutter.
A heading adds no analytical value without a relevant relationship.
Relabelling the same issue does not add an independent dimension.

lessons.task: Examine a hypothetical proposal for a community learning centre. Select three relevant dimensions, such as access, staffing and distribution of benefits. Explain how each changes the judgement and exclude one tempting but irrelevant heading.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Short- and long-term implications
lessons.explanation: Separate immediate effects from effects that depend on adaptation, maintenance or changed incentives. State uncertainty about future outcomes.
lessons.example: A new system may take training time now and might reduce repeated work later; both claims need evidence.

check.prompt: Which comparison distinguishes time horizons?
options: An assumption that implementation effects remain identical over time.
Initial training costs versus possible later processing gains.
The initial training schedule versus another description of that same schedule.
Possible future gains treated as evidence that training has no present cost.
check.explanation: It compares immediate demands with outcomes that could emerge later.
option_feedback: This assumes away the adaptation that a time-horizon comparison should examine.
It compares immediate demands with outcomes that could emerge later.
These concern the same immediate activity rather than different time horizons.
A future possibility does not erase an immediate demand.

lessons.task: Analyse a hypothetical switch to digital record handling. Separate immediate training demands from possible later changes in repeated work. Identify a maintenance condition and explain why the longer-term outcome remains uncertain.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Identifying trade-offs
lessons.explanation: A trade-off arises when improving one objective can constrain another. Explain what is gained, what may be lost and who bears the consequences.
lessons.example: Longer opening hours may improve access but require more staffing or a narrower range of services.

check.prompt: Which question tests a trade-off?
options: How many favourable comments does the proposal receive?
Can every benefit be counted while leaving the budget unchanged?
Would a clearer announcement make the proposal more appealing?
What other service might lose resources if hours are extended?
check.explanation: It examines an opportunity cost relevant to the decision.
option_feedback: Popularity does not identify the resources or services sacrificed.
Counting benefits alone does not examine the resource constraint.
Communication does not identify the competing use of staffing resources.
It examines an opportunity cost relevant to the decision.

lessons.task: A hypothetical centre has a fixed staffing budget. Compare extending opening hours with increasing support during existing hours. Explain the opportunity cost, who gains or loses and what evidence would change your preference.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Counterfactual thinking
lessons.explanation: A counterfactual asks what might happen without the proposed cause or intervention. It helps distinguish the effect of a change from an existing trend.
lessons.example: To assess a new timetable, ask how attendance might have changed under the previous timetable over the same period.

check.prompt: What is the relevant counterfactual?
options: Attendance during that period if the timetable had not changed.
Attendance before the change, regardless of the trend during the later period.
Attendance after the change, without a comparison.
The announced attendance target for the new timetable.
check.explanation: The comparison concerns the outcome in the absence of the change.
option_feedback: The comparison concerns the outcome in the absence of the change.
A previous period alone may not represent what would have happened during the same later period.
The observed outcome alone does not describe the absence of the change.
An intended target is not the outcome that would occur without the intervention.

lessons.task: A hypothetical school introduces a new timetable during a term when attendance was already changing. Specify the relevant outcome without that change, explain why the before–after comparison may mislead and propose a cautious comparison strategy.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Comparing proposed solutions
lessons.explanation: Apply consistent criteria such as feasibility, cost, access and unintended effects. State the evidence and assumptions behind each comparison.
lessons.example: Compare a later opening time with an evening trial using the same access and staffing criteria.

check.prompt: What makes a comparison fair?
options: Ranking the options by the number of benefits their supporters name.
Assessing only the preferred option against the main implementation constraint.
Using the same relevant criteria for both options.
Using a different favourable criterion for each preferred option.
check.explanation: Consistent criteria let the reader assess the trade-off.
option_feedback: A count of claimed benefits does not evaluate comparable effects or constraints.
The competing option must also be assessed against relevant criteria.
Consistent criteria let the reader assess the trade-off.
Changing criteria prevents a consistent comparison.

lessons.task: Compare two hypothetical ways to improve access: later in-person hours and an online alternative. Use the same relevant criteria for both. Distinguish known constraints from assumptions and explain a conditional preference without inventing costs.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Balanced conclusions
lessons.explanation: A balanced conclusion weighs the evidence rather than giving equal weight to every view. State the most defensible judgement and the conditions or uncertainty that remain.
lessons.example: A limited trial may be preferable if supervision is feasible; otherwise a different arrangement needs consideration.

check.prompt: Which conclusion is appropriately bounded?
options: The trial is defensible if the staffing condition can be met.
The trial must be adopted because it has at least one possible benefit.
The trial must be rejected until no uncertainty remains.
Both options deserve equal weight merely because two views were presented.
check.explanation: It takes a position while retaining a relevant condition.
option_feedback: It takes a position while retaining a relevant condition.
A possible benefit does not resolve the relevant constraint.
A bounded judgement can be possible before every uncertainty disappears.
Balance depends on the quality of support, not counting viewpoints.

lessons.task: Consider a hypothetical trial with possible access benefits but unresolved supervision constraints. Reach a bounded judgement, identify the strongest remaining objection and state what evidence could change your conclusion.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Constructing an analytical paragraph
lessons.explanation: Develop a controlling judgement, explain a mechanism, examine an alternative, state evidence needs and reach a qualified conclusion. A list of facts is insufficient.
lessons.example: Outline only: issue → mechanism → competing explanation → evidence needed → conditional judgement. The writer supplies the analysis.

check.prompt: Which element changes a descriptive list into analysis?
options: Giving each observation a separate heading without comparing explanations.
Explaining and testing relationships between the observations.
Arranging the observations chronologically without explaining their links.
Adding a quotation without examining its relevance to the mechanism.
check.explanation: Analysis depends on reasoned relationships and evidence, not length.
option_feedback: Headings do not supply the missing analytical connections.
Analysis depends on reasoned relationships and evidence, not length.
Sequence helps description, but it does not by itself explain or test a relationship.
A quotation cannot replace the causal or inferential link.

lessons.task: Write a hypothetical paragraph about delays in processing study-service requests. Explain a mechanism, contrast a competing cause, identify a discriminating observation and reach a qualified judgement. Make the connections explicit rather than listing facts.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.

lessons.title: Choose natural word combinations
lessons.explanation: A collocation is a customary combination of words: make a decision, take responsibility, raise a question. Learning the whole phrase is more useful than replacing each word with a longer synonym. A formal phrase is useful only when its meaning suits the sentence.
lessons.example: Awkward: The group did a decision. Natural: The group made a decision. The action stays the same; the verb–noun combination changes.

check.prompt: Which version uses the conventional verb–noun combination for accepting responsibility?
options: The editor achieved responsibility for the error.
The editor took responsibility for the error.
The editor did responsibility for the error.
The editor performed responsibility for the error.
check.explanation: Take responsibility is the conventional phrase for accepting accountability.
option_feedback: Achieve describes reaching a result, not accepting responsibility in this sentence.
Take responsibility is the conventional phrase for accepting accountability.
Do responsibility is not the conventional phrase for accepting accountability.
Perform can describe a task, but perform responsibility is not the intended combination.

lessons.task: Write two sentences about a study decision, using make a decision and take responsibility naturally. Explain who acts in each sentence.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Have I used each phrase with its intended meaning?
Can I name the person who acts without adding an unnecessary synonym?

lessons.title: Make pronouns and references clear
lessons.explanation: A pronoun should point to an identifiable person or thing. If two nouns could be its referent, repeat the relevant name or restructure the sentence. This and that are often clearer with a noun: this delay, that proposal. Repetition is helpful when it prevents ambiguity.
lessons.example: Unclear: Sara told Hina that her draft needed a title. Clear if Sara means Hina: Sara told Hina that Hina’s draft needed a title. The intended owner must be known before editing.

check.prompt: The intended owner is Hina. Which revision makes that meaning explicit?
options: Sara told Hina that her draft needed a title.
She told her that her draft needed a title.
Sara told Hina that Sara’s draft needed a title.
Sara told Hina that Hina’s draft needed a title.
check.explanation: Naming Hina identifies the intended owner of the draft.
option_feedback: Her can still refer to either Sara or Hina in this context.
Replacing both names with pronouns removes the information needed to identify the owner.
This version is clear but changes the intended owner from Hina to Sara.
Naming Hina identifies the intended owner of the draft.

lessons.task: Write two connected sentences about two classmates sharing notes. Make the owner of the notes explicit; use a pronoun only where its reference is clear.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Could a pronoun refer to either person?
Does my revision preserve the intended owner rather than merely remove a pronoun?

lessons.title: Give a paragraph one controlling idea
lessons.explanation: A paragraph develops a controlling idea. A useful topic sentence states the particular point the paragraph will explain, rather than announcing a broad subject. Subsequent sentences should develop that point. A related but different point may need its own paragraph.
lessons.example: Broad: Revision is important. More focused: A short review after a study session helps a learner identify points that remain unclear. The following sentences should explain that review process, not describe an unrelated exam timetable.

check.prompt: Which topic sentence sets a clear focus for a paragraph about organising a study desk?
options: There are many things in life.
This paragraph is about desks and all other furniture.
Study desks exist in different places, and examinations have many subjects.
Keeping only the materials for the current task on the desk can reduce interruptions from searching.
check.explanation: It identifies one practice and a particular effect that the paragraph can explain.
option_feedback: This is too broad to direct the paragraph’s supporting sentences.
Announcing a large collection of subjects does not identify a controlling point.
These observations do not establish the specific point the paragraph will develop.
It identifies one practice and a particular effect that the paragraph can explain.

lessons.task: Write a paragraph of at least 30 words about one practical study habit. Begin with a focused topic sentence, explain how the habit works, and finish without introducing a different habit.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Can I state my paragraph’s single focus?
Does each supporting sentence explain that focus?

lessons.title: Develop a point instead of repeating it
lessons.explanation: Support explains a point through a reason, a relevant detail or an example. Repeating a claim with stronger adjectives does not develop it. An invented practice scenario can illustrate a mechanism, but it cannot prove that all students behave that way. Label imagined situations as examples.
lessons.example: Claim: A revision log can make the next session more focused. Development: If a learner records an unresolved question, the next session can begin by addressing it rather than rereading everything. This is an explanatory example, not a measured finding.

check.prompt: Which sentence develops the claim that clear file names make notes easier to locate?
options: Every learner always benefits equally from any naming system.
Clear file names are useful because useful file names are clear.
A label containing the subject and topic lets a learner identify the required file without opening every document.
Clear file names are very, very useful.
check.explanation: It explains the connection between the naming practice and locating a file.
option_feedback: This adds an unsupported universal claim rather than a defensible explanation.
This is circular wording: it restates the claim as its reason.
It explains the connection between the naming practice and locating a file.
Intensifying the adjective repeats the claim without explaining it.

lessons.task: Write at least 30 words explaining how a learner could use a question log. Give one explicitly hypothetical example and connect it to your point without inventing success rates.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Have I explained how my example supports the point?
Have I labelled an imagined example and avoided invented results?

lessons.title: Connect sentences through clear references
lessons.explanation: Cohesion helps readers follow a paragraph. Repeat an important term where needed, use clear pronoun references, and move from familiar information to new information. A connector cannot repair a missing logical relationship. Prefer an explicit link to a chain of vague words such as this, it and things.
lessons.example: A learner marked two unclear definitions. These definitions became the focus of the next review. Repeating definitions makes the reference explicit without an unnecessary transition.

check.prompt: Which continuation clearly refers back to the identified problem?
options: Despite this, therefore, however.
This missing date makes it difficult to identify the correct edition.
This makes it do that.
Furthermore, different matters are different.
check.explanation: This missing date names the problem and explains why it matters.
option_feedback: A string of connectors contains no claim for the reader to follow.
This missing date names the problem and explains why it matters.
The pronouns do not identify either the problem or its consequence.
A transition plus an unrelated statement does not create a meaningful connection.

lessons.task: Write at least 30 words about an incomplete set of study notes. Name one specific gap, refer to it clearly in the next sentence, and explain a practical response.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Does each this or it have a clear referent?
Does the next sentence develop information the reader can identify?

lessons.title: Explain a process in a useful order
lessons.explanation: A process paragraph presents steps in the order needed to perform a task. State the starting condition, explain the steps, and identify the result to check. First, next and finally can help, but the actions themselves must be complete. Do not confuse instructions with a claim that the process always succeeds.
lessons.example: To review a short passage, first read it without taking notes. Next, identify its main point. Finally, reread it to check whether that point accounts for the supporting details. The example describes actions, not a guaranteed score.

check.prompt: Which instruction sequence respects the stated task of checking a saved draft?
options: First be excellent, next be perfect, finally be successful.
Open the saved draft, compare it with your intended meaning, then save any revision as a new version.
Save an unknown revision, then decide which draft you meant to open.
Compare the draft before opening or reading it.
check.explanation: The reader can perform the actions in this order and retain the original draft.
option_feedback: These are aspirations rather than actions that explain the process.
The reader can perform the actions in this order and retain the original draft.
The revision is saved before its source and intended meaning are identified.
The reader needs access to the draft before comparing its wording.

lessons.task: Write at least 30 words explaining how you would check a paragraph before submitting it. Include a starting point, ordered actions and a final check.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Could another learner perform my steps in the stated order?
Have I specified a check rather than promised a result?

lessons.title: Compare like with like
lessons.explanation: A comparison uses the same relevant criterion for both items. Decide whether to discuss each item in turn or compare one criterion at a time. Words such as whereas and similarly should reflect a real contrast or similarity. Do not invent findings to make one option sound stronger.
lessons.example: In a hypothetical choice, one study space is quiet but distant; another is nearby but noisy. Comparing noise with noise and travel with travel helps the writer explain a conditional preference.

check.prompt: Which comparison uses the same criterion for both hypothetical rooms?
options: Room A is obviously better because it is Room A.
Both rooms must have identical lighting because both are rooms.
Room A has a desk lamp, whereas Room B relies on a ceiling light.
Room A has a lamp, whereas Room B is available on Tuesday.
check.explanation: Both sides describe lighting, so the reader can compare that feature.
option_feedback: This gives no criterion that supports the judgement.
A shared category does not establish an identical feature.
Both sides describe lighting, so the reader can compare that feature.
Lighting and availability are different criteria; whereas implies a comparison not supplied here.

lessons.task: Write at least 35 words comparing two imaginary study spaces using the same two criteria. State a preference that depends on a learner’s needs, not a universal ranking.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Have I applied each criterion to both options?
