Does my preference follow from the comparison and its stated conditions?

lessons.title: Acknowledge a limitation without losing your point
lessons.explanation: A concession recognises a valid limitation or alternative. It should change the strength or scope of a claim where necessary. Although and however can signal the relationship, but they cannot supply it. Do not make the concession merely decorative by repeating an absolute conclusion afterwards.
lessons.example: Although a shared reading room may offer a quieter space, its opening hours may exclude some learners. A useful recommendation must therefore specify whose schedule it suits. This hypothetical example qualifies the recommendation.

check.prompt: Which conclusion genuinely incorporates the stated limitation that a room closes at 5 pm?
options: Although it closes at 5 pm, closing times never matter to anyone.
However, therefore, the room is a room.
The room may suit learners who can study before 5 pm.
The room suits every learner regardless of schedule.
check.explanation: The recommendation is narrowed to learners whose schedules fit the stated hours.
option_feedback: This dismisses the limitation without giving a reason for doing so.
Connectors alone do not show how the limitation affects a recommendation.
The recommendation is narrowed to learners whose schedules fit the stated hours.
Every learner ignores the very scheduling limitation being considered.

lessons.task: Write at least 40 words recommending a hypothetical shared study arrangement. Acknowledge one genuine limitation and adjust the recommendation to account for it.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Does the limitation change the scope of my recommendation?
Have I avoided claiming that one arrangement suits everyone?

lessons.title: Distinguish a source from your inference
lessons.explanation: Attribution tells readers where a claim comes from. Your explanation of what it might mean is a separate inference. Preserve the source’s scope and uncertainty. If you have not verified a source, mark the claim as unverified rather than inventing an author, date or quotation.
lessons.example: Practice notice: “The reading room closes at 5 pm on Fridays.” Accurate report: The practice notice states the Friday closing time. Separate inference: This could constrain a learner who arrives later. The notice does not establish how many learners are affected.

check.prompt: What can be reported from the practice notice alone?
options: The stated Friday closing time is 5 pm.
Most learners cannot use the room on Fridays.
The closing time has reduced examination scores.
The room always closes at 5 pm on every day.
check.explanation: This reports exactly the information supplied by the notice.
option_feedback: This reports exactly the information supplied by the notice.
The notice supplies no attendance or schedule evidence about most learners.
No examination outcomes or causal evidence are supplied.
The notice specifies Fridays, so extending it to every day changes its scope.

lessons.task: Using only the fictional practice notice in the example, write at least 35 words that clearly separate its stated information, one possible implication and the additional evidence needed to assess that implication.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Have I kept the source’s day and scope unchanged?
Can the reader distinguish the source statement from my inference and evidence needs?

lessons.title: Change the wording while keeping the meaning
lessons.explanation: Paraphrasing restates meaning in a different structure and wording. Keep who acts, what happens, the time frame and any conditions. A shorter version that removes a qualification can be inaccurate. Replacing individual words with synonyms is not enough if the structure remains copied.
lessons.example: Original teaching sentence: Students may borrow a reference copy if the librarian approves the request. Faithful paraphrase: Borrowing a reference copy is possible for students with the librarian’s approval. May and the approval condition remain.

check.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the condition in “The group can meet online if every member agrees”?
options: The group has never held an online meeting.
An online meeting is possible with the agreement of all group members.
The group must meet online regardless of anyone’s view.
Some members have already agreed to meet online.
check.explanation: Possible preserves can, and agreement of all members preserves the if condition.
option_feedback: The original says nothing about the group’s previous meetings.
Possible preserves can, and agreement of all members preserves the if condition.
Must and regardless remove the original possibility and condition.
The original sentence does not report an actual agreement by any member.

lessons.task: Paraphrase these two original teaching sentences: “A learner may change the revision plan if a topic remains unclear.” “The tutor checks the new plan before the next session.” Then explain how your wording preserves permission, the condition and the sequence.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Have I retained may, if and before in meaning?
Have I avoided adding a result or event absent from the originals?

lessons.title: Open with a focus and close with a consequence
lessons.explanation: An opening should orient the reader and identify the particular issue. A closing should draw together the point developed rather than add a major unsupported claim. Avoid grand claims about all human history when a specific introduction will do. A conclusion may be qualified if the discussion is qualified.
lessons.example: Hypothetical opening: This paragraph considers how an unclear note-taking system can slow a later review. Matching close: A consistent label may therefore help retrieval, provided the learner uses it regularly. The close returns to the specific issue and retains a condition.

check.prompt: Which closing fits a paragraph that explains a possible benefit of a revision log without measuring its outcomes?
options: A revision log may help organise the next session, although its actual effect still needs checking.
Revision logs guarantee the highest examination marks.
This proves every educational problem has now been solved.
A new and unrelated claim about national transport follows.
check.explanation: It draws a bounded implication consistent with the paragraph’s limited support.
option_feedback: It draws a bounded implication consistent with the paragraph’s limited support.
A possible organisational benefit does not establish guaranteed examination results.
A limited discussion cannot support a universal claim about education.
A closing should synthesise the paragraph rather than introduce a disconnected major issue.

lessons.task: Write at least 45 words about a hypothetical revision log, including a focused opening, an explanation and a qualified closing. Do not claim measured improvements.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Does the opening identify the issue the paragraph actually develops?
Does the closing follow from the explanation without adding unsupported success claims?

lessons.title: Revise meaning, structure and language in separate passes
lessons.explanation: Editing is easier when each pass has a purpose. First check meaning and missing conditions. Next check sentence order and paragraph focus. Then check agreement, tense, punctuation and word choice. Finally compare the revision with the original. A change is useful when it makes the intended meaning clearer; fewer words alone do not establish improvement.
lessons.example: Draft: Because the learner had little time. She did a decision to skip all review. Revision: Because she had little time, the learner decided to shorten the review. The fragment and phrase are repaired, but skipping all review became shortening it: that meaning change needs the writer’s explicit approval.

check.prompt: What must the editor notice about the worked revision?
options: It preserves every detail exactly because it is more fluent.
A fluent sentence is always factually more accurate.
Only the number of words matters when comparing revisions.
It repairs language but changes skipping all review into shortening the review.
check.explanation: Both the repair and the changed action must be identified; fluency does not authorise a meaning change.
option_feedback: Fluency does not preserve the distinction between skipping and shortening.
Grammatical fluency cannot establish the factual accuracy of a statement.
Word count cannot show whether an action or qualification has been changed.
Both the repair and the changed action must be identified; fluency does not authorise a meaning change.

lessons.task: Write an original paragraph of at least 50 words about organising your next study session. In your review, name one meaning check, one structure check and one language check. Save a revision independently, then compare which changes improve clarity and which alter your intention.
lessons.attribution: Original CSS Vista instructional example; not an authentic past-paper question.
self_review: Have I checked that the revision still says what I intended?
Can I explain a specific improvement without treating a shorter version as automatically better?
